\section{Abstract}\label{abstract}

Guard models are deployed quantized. Whether that changes their verdicts is usually settled with a
net rate delta, and concurrent work shows why that is the weakest available evidence: a net delta is
the residue after opposing per-item changes cancel, and cancellation is most complete exactly where
equivalence claims are made {[}Certify{]}.

We apply their paired-equivalence instrument to five guard classifiers from three publishers across a
seven-level GGUF ladder --- 35 cells, 1,000 shared items, per-item verdicts, each compared against that
model\textquotesingle s own \texttt{F16} reference.

\textbf{Five results.}

\textbf{First, their headline ratio does not transfer, though smaller than Draft 1 claimed.} Computed as
they compute it --- the median of finite cellwise ratios --- guard verdict churn runs \textbf{1.86$\times$ the net
accuracy delta} against their \textbf{3.85$\times$}. \warn{} Draft 1 reported 1.4$\times$ against their 5.40$\times$, comparing a
cellwise median to a ratio-of-medians and partitioning by verdict direction rather than by
correctness. \textbf{Both figures are now computed both ways against their matching statistic} (ratio of
medians: ours 2.75$\times$, theirs 5.40$\times$).

\textbf{Second, and this is the strongest result here: the evidential crisis their paper documents does not
occur in this domain.} They report the share of cells that are neither certifiable at the registered
$\pm$2pp margin nor detectably different --- the gray zone where an evaluation cannot answer the question a
release note answers --- at \textbf{69.2\%} of their 1,398-cell first stratum and \textbf{77.7\%} of the second.
\textbf{For the guard ladder it is 0.0\%.} Every one of 30 cells is either provably equivalent at $\pm$2pp
(70.0\%) or detectably different (30.0\%). Guard verdicts churn little enough that 1,000 items settles
the question, where a general-model benchmark of the same size cannot.

\textbf{Third, and this is what a symmetric accuracy metric structurally cannot see: quantization has a
safety direction, and the model picks it, not the bit-width.} On the same ladder, ShieldGemma 9B
loses almost only unsafe detections (\textbf{144 unsafe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}safe against 4 the other way, 0.97}) while
Qwen3Guard 4B almost only over-blocks (\textbf{0.33}). ShieldGemma 2B \textbf{reverses mid-ladder}: purely
usability-adverse at \texttt{Q4\_K\_M} and \texttt{Q3\_K\_M} (0 unsafe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}safe in both), then \textbf{47-to-1 safety-adverse at
\texttt{Q2\_K}}. A deployer cannot infer which way a guard will fail from the precision it is served at.

\textbf{Fourth, applying {[}Certify{]}\textquotesingle s certification sizing to guards reproduces their central conceptual
point in a new domain: the requirement tracks churn, not quality.} The worst guard we measure (FNR
0.857) and a mid-range one (FNR 0.280) require \textbf{identical} evidence --- 1,113 items at a $\pm$1
percentage-point margin --- while the best (FNR 0.028) needs 248. \textbf{Three of five models need more items
than the 1,000 this evaluation ran}, so a benchmark of this size cannot certify them at $\pm$1pp.

\textbf{Fifth, the mechanism for that direction exists in the literature, it is not ours, and we tested
whether it reaches guards at all.} {[}MarginShrink{]} fit a proportional damage law, \emph{m\textquotesingle{}} = \emph{c\textperiodcentered{}m} + \emph{b} + $\varepsilon$,
on 16 generative instruct models; \textbf{no guard classifier appears in their study, nor in {[}Certify{]} or
{[}QualityProxy{]}}. We captured decision margins for two guards across seven precisions and find the law
\textbf{transfers}: the multiplicative form beats a constant-additive one in 5 of 6 cells in both models,
and their flip predictor --- fitted on margins, never on flips --- predicts guard flip rates to \textbf{0.75 and
0.94 percentage points} against their 1.7pp median. The fitted push \emph{b} \textbf{disagrees in sign between
the two guards and reverses within a single ladder}, which is the shape of the behavior in the third
result. \warn{} \textbf{This test required a different serving stack}, because the GGUF stack cannot expose
logits at all, so it establishes the law for guards as a class rather than for the cells above. \textbf{Its
pre-registered monotonicity check failed and is reported as failed.}

We also report a concern of our own that did not survive testing. Prior work in this program recorded
that the serving-noise floor is not a single number: on verdict-selected sets it ran 1.0--5.7\%, which
would have left \textbf{27 of 30 cells} indistinguishable from noise. Rather than argue which floor
applies, we measured it on this corpus with eight same-configuration replicates, deliberately choosing
the model whose churn most favored the null. \textbf{The floor is 0.107\% --- two unstable items in a thousand
--- the stratified figure, not the borderline one. The concern was wrong.}

\textbf{Keywords:} guard models, quantization, model compression, equivalence testing, safety evaluation,
measurement study

\section{1. What this paper is}\label{1-what-this-paper-is}

\textbf{The method is {[}Certify{]}\textquotesingle s and we apply it.} Their five-line reporting standard is explicitly
general --- \emph{"It applies to any comparison between two models alike enough to be worth comparing"} --- and
this is an application of it, not a competitor to it.

\textbf{A borrowed instrument is not a borrowed result.} We say this once, plainly, because the
alternative reading would misplace the paper. {[}Certify{]}\textquotesingle s atlas is benchmark accuracy and
{[}QualityProxy{]}\textquotesingle s outcome is a generative model\textquotesingle s refusal scored by an LLM judge. \textbf{Neither measures a
guard classifier} --- the component that actually sits in the request path and whose verdict \emph{is} the
decision rather than something a judge infers from a generation. Applying their instrument there
produces findings neither could have observed, and two of the three below are work the sources
\textbf{named as outstanding and did not do}.

\textbf{Three things remain, and we claim only these:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Directional churn} (\S{}5.2). {[}Certify{]}\textquotesingle s churn is symmetric by construction, because
  correct$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}wrong and wrong$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}correct are the same kind of event on a benchmark. \textbf{On a guard they are
  not}: \texttt{unsafe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}safe} admits harmful content, \texttt{safe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}unsafe} only over-blocks. This decomposition is
  unavailable in their setting, and it turns out to carry the paper\textquotesingle s most actionable finding.
\item
  \textbf{A measured floor for the corpus the claims are made on} (\S{}5.6). {[}Certify{]} size their tests from
  disagreement observed \emph{under compression}. We add an independently measured
  \emph{same-configuration} floor, which is a different quantity and which their toolkit does not carry.
\item
  \textbf{Two extensions the prior art explicitly asks for.} {[}QualityProxy{]} \S{}5.3 names its own equivalence
  gap --- \emph{it does not run a formal two-one-sided-tests procedure for every cell}, and directs readers
  needing a certified statement to \emph{"apply a targeted TOST to the specific metric, model, and
  quantization cell of interest."} \textbf{\S{}5.5 does that for all 30 cells.} {[}Certify{]} \S{}3.6 requires that
  the test they size actually be run; \textbf{\S{}5.5 runs it.} Neither is a novel instrument; both are work
  the sources named as outstanding.
\item
  \textbf{A test of whether the known mechanism reaches this object} (\S{}5.8). {[}MarginShrink{]}\textquotesingle s damage law
  is fitted entirely on generative instruct models. \textbf{Whether it governs a classifier whose verdict
  \emph{is} the decision was untested by them or by anyone}, and an earlier draft of this paper listed it
  as a gap we could not close. We closed it. \textbf{The law is theirs; the measurement of its reach, and
  one negative result inside it, are ours.}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{We claim no novelty on:} the churn-versus-net-delta argument, the cancellation account, TOST
certification sizing, the observation that aggregate scores conceal per-item movement, or the
cross-scheme safety audit. \textbf{All are prior art}, cited at first use.

\warn{} \textbf{Our first hypothesis was not blind.} The M3 and M3-X per-item verdicts existed on disk before
this study was designed, and their headline --- 4 to 18 verdicts per thousand differing at \texttt{Q4\_K\_M} ---
was known. \S{}5.1 is confirmatory of an expectation already formed. \S{}5.2 and \S{}5.4 were not.

\section{2. Related work}\label{2-related-work}

\textbf{{[}Certify{]}} audits 17 published equivalence claims from three registered sampling frames and finds
none declares a prospective numerical margin and none releases task-matched per-item outputs. Its
atlas puts churn at \textasciitilde5$\times$ the net delta across 1,707 cells spanning 1.3B to 405B parameters. Its
controlled experiment pairs GPTQ and AWQ on byte-identical calibration samples across five seeds and
finds the method ordering reverses with the calibration draw in 5 of 8 confirmatory cells.

\textbf{Two of their framing points are load-bearing here and we adopt both.} \emph{Detection is not
certification}: failing to reject a difference is not evidence of equivalence, and their registration
commits to not reading it that way. And their sizing equation \emph{"answers how many items would this
benchmark need for an equivalence test to have 80\% power, given how much models of this kind disagree
item-by-item. It does not answer how many items would certify the delta this source observed."} \textbf{Both
constrain how \S{}5.3 and \S{}5.4 may be read, and are restated there.}

\textbf{{[}QualityProxy{]}} tests whether quality metrics proxy for safety across GGUF, AWQ and GPTQ, finding
9 hidden-danger rows in 51 where quality is flat or improving while refusal degrades 12 to 68 points,
concentrated in AWQ and GPTQ. \textbf{Its safety measurement is a generative model\textquotesingle s refusal, labeled by an
LLM judge} (primary \texttt{gemma3:12b}, secondary Claude Sonnet 4, Cohen\textquotesingle s $\kappa$ = 0.873).

\textbf{{[}MarginShrink{]}} supplies the mechanism this paper does not. Across \textbf{16 models from 8 families}
and four quantization schemes, plus activation and KV-cache axes, they show compression damage is
\textbf{proportional rather than additive}: the quantized margin follows \emph{m$'$} = \emph{c\textperiodcentered{}m} + \emph{b} + $\varepsilon$, the
surviving fraction \emph{c} collapsing from a median 0.86 at 4 bits to \textbf{0.00 at 2}. A directional push
\emph{b} accompanies it, producing \textbf{one-directional collapse} --- 96\% of should-call decisions flip while
80\% of should-not-call survive. From the fitted law they derive a flip predictor accurate to a
\textbf{median 1.7 percentage points} on held-out cells. They also report that transferring the fitted
constants between models gives \textbf{18--33 point errors at 3 bits}, so the law must be re-measured per
model and bit-width.

\textbf{The gap all three leave is the same one.} A guard classifier is not a generator being judged and
not a next-token choice between two continuations; \textbf{its verdict is the measurement}. That removes
the judge from the loop --- no grader variance, no $\kappa$ --- and it introduces an asymmetry none of the three
outcome variables has. \textbf{{[}MarginShrink{]}\textquotesingle s 16 models are all generative instruct models and no guard
classifier appears in any of the three studies.}

\warn{} \textbf{This bounds our contribution rather than widening it.} Directional compression damage is
{[}MarginShrink{]}\textquotesingle s (\S{}5.2), and the mechanism for it is theirs (\S{}7.7). What we add is the object, the
equivalence framing, and a measured floor --- not the phenomenon.

\textbf{Prior results this paper depends on.} The corpus, the ladder and all 35 cells of per-item verdicts
come from earlier pre-registered experiments in this program {[}T-03 \S{}5.4, \S{}5.8{]}. The serving-floor
methodology is {[}T-03 \S{}5.10{]}, and the hazard that motivated \S{}5.5 is its \texttt{R42}.

\section{3. Setting}\label{3-setting}

\textbf{Object.} Five input-side guard classifiers from three publishers: Llama Guard 3 8B, ShieldGemma 2B
and 9B, Qwen3Guard-Gen 0.6B and 4B.

\textbf{Ladder.} Seven precisions from one publisher\textquotesingle s conversion pipeline --- \texttt{F16}, \texttt{Q8\_0}, \texttt{Q6\_K},
\texttt{Q5\_K\_M}, \texttt{Q4\_K\_M}, \texttt{Q3\_K\_M}, \texttt{Q2\_K} --- so the conversion pipeline is held constant and only the
precision varies. Each model is compared \textbf{against its own \texttt{F16}}, never against another model.

\textbf{Corpus.} 1,000 items, 533 unsafe, 467 benign, identical across all 35 cells, byte-identical file
verified by hash. \texttt{num\_ctx} 8192, \texttt{seed} 0, one serving stack throughout.

\warn{} \textbf{491 of the 1,000 items are adversarial by construction.} Absolute rates here are not deployment
rates and must not be quoted as guard performance. Every quantity below is a \emph{within-model} delta, so
the corpus composition cancels.

\section{4. Method}\label{4-method}

\textbf{Quantities}, fixed in a pre-registration frozen at \texttt{9f9d53d0} before any churn figure was computed:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{net delta} --- change in FNR and FPR, \textbf{reported separately, never pooled}
\item
  \textbf{churn} --- items whose binary verdict differs from that model\textquotesingle s own \texttt{F16} on the same input
\item
  \textbf{directional churn} --- \texttt{unsafe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}safe} and \texttt{safe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}unsafe}, \textbf{always separately}
\item
  \textbf{required n} --- TOST sizing at declared margins, following {[}Certify{]}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Certification sizing}, implemented as {[}Certify{]} \S{}3.2 specify:

\begin{verbatim}
sd_paired = sqrt(p_d)
n_req = ceil( ((z_(1-alpha) + z_(1-beta)) * sd_paired / m)^2 )
\end{verbatim}

at one-sided $\alpha$ = .05 (z = 1.6449) and 80\% power (z = 0.8416). \textbf{We verified our implementation
numerically against their published Table 1} rather than against our reading of their abstract: their
\texttt{musr} row at a $\pm$2pp margin reproduces to 520 against their printed 519, the residual being display
rounding of the discordance rate.

\textbf{Stability guard.} The churn ratio is undefined at a zero net delta and meaningless below a few
items. \textbf{Cells with a net delta under 3 items report raw counts with the ratio suppressed}, fixed
before any cell was computed.

\textbf{Unit of inference.} Items here are independent --- 1,000 flat identifiers with distinct source
indices and no variant clustering --- so paired item-level McNemar is valid and no cluster bootstrap is
used. This differs from other corpora in this program and is stated because it changes what is valid.

\section{5. Results}\label{5-results}

\subsection{5.1 The ratio does not transfer, and Draft 1 compared the wrong number}\label{51-the-ratio-does-not-transfer-and-draft-1-compared-the-wrong-number}

\rmark{R1} {[}Certify{]} \S{}4.2 is explicit that two different statistics are in play:

\begin{quote}
These are ratios of medians, not medians of cellwise ratios, and the two summarise different
things. The median among finite cellwise ratios is 3.85.

--- {[}Certify{]} \S{}4.2. \emph{Quoted verbatim; the source spelling stands.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Both are computed here against their matching figure:}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
statistic & guards (this work) & {[}Certify{]} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
median of finite \textbf{cellwise} ratios & \textbf{1.86$\times$} & \textbf{3.85$\times$} \\
\textbf{ratio of medians} & \textbf{2.75$\times$} & \textbf{5.40$\times$} \\
\end{longtable}

\warn{} \textbf{Draft 1 reported 1.4$\times$ against 5.40$\times$} --- a cellwise median against a ratio-of-medians, and
computed on a net delta partitioned by \emph{verdict} direction rather than by \emph{correctness}. Their net
delta is an accuracy delta. \textbf{Corrected, the gap is about 2$\times$, not about 4$\times$.}

\warn{} \textbf{We also tested whether arm separation explained the gap, and it does not.} The pre-registration
keeps the FNR and FPR arms apart, and arm separation prevents exactly the cancellation their critique
concerns --- so we recomputed pooled. The conclusion survives the correction: \textbf{guard verdicts churn
roughly half as much, relative to net movement, as benchmark accuracy does.}

Offered as a hypothesis and not a finding: a binary verdict on a fixed input has less room for
opposing flips than a generated answer scored for correctness.

\warn{} \textbf{This does not weaken their argument; it locates it.} Cancellation is still present at 1.86$\times$, and
a guard benchmark reporting one pooled number still hides it.

\subsection{5.2 Direction is a model property, not a bit-width property}\label{52-direction-is-a-model-property-not-a-bit-width-property}

\rmark{R2} Directional churn pooled over the ladder:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
model & unsafe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}safe & safe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}unsafe & share u$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}s & reading \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\textbf{shieldgemma-9b} & \textbf{144} & \textbf{4} & \textbf{0.97} & \textbf{safety-adverse} \\
llamaguard3-8b & 78 & 76 & 0.51 & symmetric \\
qwen3guard-06b & 247 & 306 & 0.45 & symmetric \\
shieldgemma-2b & 56 & 71 & 0.44 & symmetric \\
\textbf{qwen3guard-4b} & \textbf{15} & \textbf{30} & \textbf{0.33} & \textbf{usability-adverse} \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{The same seven-precision ladder drives two models in opposite directions.} ShieldGemma 9B loses
almost exclusively unsafe detections; Qwen3Guard 4B almost exclusively over-blocks.

\rmark{R3} \textbf{And one model reverses within its own ladder.} ShieldGemma 2B is \emph{purely} usability-adverse at
\texttt{Q4\_K\_M} (0 unsafe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}safe, 18 safe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}unsafe) and at \texttt{Q3\_K\_M} (0 against 41) --- then flips at \texttt{Q2\_K} to
\textbf{47 unsafe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}safe against 1}. \textbf{Direction is not even monotone in precision within a single model.}

\textbf{Why this is unavailable to {[}Certify{]}\textquotesingle s instrument, and to {[}QualityProxy{]}\textquotesingle s.} Their outcome is
symmetric: an item going correct$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}wrong is the same kind of event as wrong$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}correct, and a churn count
is the natural summary. \textbf{A guard\textquotesingle s two directions have opposite consequences}, so a single churn
number for ShieldGemma 9B --- 148 items --- describes a model that has become materially less safe and one
that has become materially noisier equally well. \textbf{It is the wrong summary, and only a guard-shaped
outcome variable exposes that.}

\warn{} \textbf{Directional compression damage is not new, and {[}MarginShrink{]} must be credited for it.} They
fit a \textbf{directional push} term \emph{b} alongside a margin-shrinkage coefficient, and report
\textbf{one-directional collapse} at the bit-width where damage begins: 96\% of should-call decisions flip
while 80\% of should-not-call survive, so a compressed agent \textbf{stops acting rather than acting wrongly}.
They also measure safety-refusal loss by model size --- a 1.7B model loses almost all refusals at 3
bits, a 4B some, a 32B none.

\textbf{What is left to us is narrower than "direction," and we state it as the narrower thing.} Their \emph{b}
is fitted per model, decision family and bit-width, and their directional result is \emph{within} a model
across decision types. \textbf{Ours is across models on one decision type}: the same seven-precision ladder
drives ShieldGemma 9B and Qwen3Guard 4B in \textbf{opposite} directions on the same corpus. And
ShieldGemma 2B \textbf{reverses within its own ladder}, which is permitted by their per-cell fit --- a sign
change in \emph{b} between bit-widths --- but is not something their reported results exhibit or predict.

\textbf{\S{}5.8 returns to this and fits \emph{b} directly.} A sign reversal within one guard\textquotesingle s ladder is not
merely permitted by their model; \textbf{we measure it, in both guards we instrument.} \warn{} On a different
stack, so it supplies the \emph{shape} of an explanation for this table rather than a fitted account of it.

\subsection{5.3 What the McNemar column may not be used for}\label{53-what-the-mcnemar-column-may-not-be-used-for}

\rmark{R4} Per-cell McNemar exact tests are reported in the artifact. \warn{} \textbf{A large \emph{p} here is not evidence
of equivalence}, and we adopt {[}Certify{]}\textquotesingle s registered commitment verbatim: \emph{failing to find evidence
of a difference is not evidence of equivalence; with a small enough evaluation, nothing is
detectable.} The cells with high \emph{p} are cells where this evaluation cannot detect a difference,
which is a statement about the evaluation. \S{}5.4 is the instrument that answers the other question.

\subsection{5.4 Certification: the requirement tracks churn, not guard quality}\label{54-certification-the-requirement-tracks-churn-not-guard-quality}

\rmark{R5} Items required to certify equivalence at a declared margin, at the deployed default \texttt{Q4\_K\_M}:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllll@{}}

shieldgemma-2b & \textbf{0.8574} & 0.0180 & \textbf{1,113} & 279 \\

\rmark{R6} \textbf{{[}Certify{]}\textquotesingle s central conceptual point reproduces in a new domain.} They show the requirement is
set by churn rather than by benchmark difficulty --- MMLU needs three times GPQA\textquotesingle s items despite being
the easier task. \textbf{The guard analog is sharper because the quality gap is larger.} ShieldGemma 2B
misses 85.7\% of this corpus and Llama Guard 3 misses 28.0\%; \textbf{they require exactly the same evidence},
1,113 items. Qwen3Guard 4B, which misses 2.8\%, requires \textbf{a quarter of that}. \textbf{A practitioner cannot
size a guard equivalence evaluation from the guard\textquotesingle s accuracy, its size, or its family. Only from its
churn.}

\rmark{R7} \textbf{Three of five models need more than the 1,000 items this evaluation ran} to support a $\pm$1pp
claim. That is a fact about the evaluation, not a defect in the models.

\warn{} \textbf{What this table is not.} Following {[}Certify{]} \S{}3.2, it is the planning size for 80\% power under
an assumed \textbf{true difference of zero}. \textbf{It does not tell you how many items would certify the delta
we actually observed}, and must not be read that way. Their \S{}3.6 adds the constraint Draft 1 missed:
\textbf{meeting the count makes the test informative, it does not certify anything on its own --- the test
still has to be run and to pass.} \S{}5.5 runs it.

\warn{} \textbf{Their \S{}3.5 also fixes which path we are on.} The guard ladder has no row in their Table 1, and
for a benchmark with no row their step 2 prescribes measuring discordance on your own pair and using
their equations directly. \textbf{That is what we did}, so the figures above are point requirements from
one observed discordance per model --- not the p25/median/p75 band their families carry, and not an
extrapolation from their atlas.

\subsection{5.5 The test, actually run --- and a gray zone that is empty}\label{55-the-test-actually-run--and-a-gray-zone-that-is-empty}

\warn{} \textbf{Draft 1 reported required sample sizes and stopped there.} {[}Certify{]} \S{}3.6 forecloses that:
\emph{"any claim that a model meeting these counts is equivalent {[}is not supported{]}, because meeting the
count makes the test informative, and the test still has to be run and to pass."} \textbf{We ran it.}

\rmark{R8} \textbf{The framework applies to guards by an identity worth stating.} Their \S{}3.5 requires only that
the harness assign each item a correct-or-incorrect state, and explicitly excludes LLM-as-judge
ratings, graded scores and perplexity measures. A guard verdict qualifies --- and \textbf{for binary
classification against a binary label, verdict disagreement and correctness disagreement are the same
event}, because differing verdicts mean exactly one is right. \textbf{Our churn is therefore exactly their
\texttt{p\_d}.} We assert this in code rather than assume it: it holds in all 30 cells.

\rmark{R9} \textbf{TOST at the registered $\pm$2pp margin, run on all 30 cells}, with the 90\% two-sided interval on
the paired accuracy delta required to fall inside the margin. Placed on their Table 2 scale:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
population & certifiable @ $\pm$2pp & detectable (McNemar \emph{p}\textless.05) & \textbf{gray zone} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
{[}Certify{]} S1 --- 1,398 cells & 4.9\% & 26.5\% & \textbf{69.2\%} \\
{[}Certify{]} S2 --- 309 cells & 17.2\% & 6.1\% & \textbf{77.7\%} \\
\textbf{P8 guard ladder --- 30 cells} & \textbf{70.0\%} & \textbf{30.0\%} & \textbf{0.0\%} \\
\end{longtable}

\textbf{The gray zone is empty.} {[}Certify{]}\textquotesingle s empirical core is that the modal compressed-model cell is one
where \emph{"the evaluation cannot answer the question the release note answers"} --- 69.2\% and 77.7\% of
their two strata. \textbf{For guard classifiers at n = 1,000, no cell is in that state.} Every one is
either provably equivalent at the margin or detectably different.

\textbf{This is a contribution to their framework rather than a challenge to it}, and it follows directly
from \S{}5.1: the requirement scales with churn, guards churn about half as much, and 1,000 items is
therefore enough where for a general-model benchmark it is not. \textbf{Certifying a quantized guard is
cheap. Certifying a quantized general model is not.}

\warn{} \textbf{A cell can be both certifiable and detectable} --- a real difference, provably smaller than the
margin --- so the shares do not sum to one. At the stricter $\pm$1pp margin the certifiable share falls,
which is \S{}5.4\textquotesingle s point restated: the margin is a declared choice with quadratic cost.

\rmark{R10} \textbf{Their \S{}4.3 phenomenon occurs more often in guards and matters less.} They report 145 of 1,707
cells (8.49\%) scoring \emph{identically} to baseline while still disagreeing item by item, at a median
churn of 0.0720. \textbf{Four of our 30 cells (13.3\%) move accuracy by under one item while churning} ---
proportionally more --- but at a median churn of \textbf{0.0060, an order of magnitude smaller}. The
cancellation is real in guards and its magnitude is not.

\subsection{5.6 A concern of ours, tested and refuted}\label{56-a-concern-of-ours-tested-and-refuted}

\rmark{R11} Against this program\textquotesingle s stratified serving-noise floor of 0.09\% {[}T-03 \S{}5.10{]}, 29 of 30 cells
clear. \warn{} \textbf{That comparison is nearly vacuous at n = 1,000}: 0.09\% is 0.9 items, so any cell with a
single churned item passes. It was run as pre-registered and it decides almost nothing.

\rmark{R12} \warn{} \textbf{We then raised a concern that would have undercut the entire paper.} T-03 \texttt{R42} records
that the floor is probably not one number: on sets \textbf{selected by a prior verdict} it ran \textbf{1.0--5.7\%},
which is 10--57 items here. Against that floor \textbf{27 of 30 cells do not clear}, and every deployed-default
\texttt{Q4\_K\_M} effect in \S{}5.2 would be indistinguishable from serving noise.

\textbf{Rather than argue which floor applies, we measured it} (addendum \texttt{69f3028f}, frozen before the
runs). Eight same-configuration replicates --- identical model, quantization, corpus, seed, context,
separate containers. \textbf{Qwen3Guard 4B at \texttt{Q4\_K\_M} was chosen because it had the lowest churn on the
entire ladder, making it the case where a floor most plausibly explains the effect.} Choosing the
condition that most favors the null was deliberate and was stated in the addendum before the runs.

\rmark{R13} \textbf{The floor on this corpus is 0.107\% mean pairwise disagreement --- 1.07 items in 1,000 --- with
just 2 items ever unstable across all eight runs} (Wilson 95\% {[}0.055\%, 0.726\%{]}).

\textbf{That is the stratified figure, not the borderline one. Our concern was wrong.} Adversarial
\emph{weighting} does not raise the floor the way verdict \emph{selection} does: the borderline sets were
borderline because every item had been caught and then evaded, which selects for proximity to a
decision boundary. A corpus that merely contains adversarial text does not.

\textbf{The pre-registered conclusion stands, now against a floor measured on the corpus the claim is made
on rather than imported from another one.}

\warn{} \textbf{It stands narrowly for the condition measured.} A 4-item effect against 2 ever-unstable items is
a factor of two --- above the floor, not comfortably. The models showing 17--18 items at \texttt{Q4\_K\_M} are
clearly above \textbf{if their floors are comparable, and floors are model-dependent} {[}T-03 \texttt{R41}{]}, so that
is an assumption.

\subsection{5.7 Ladder position}\label{57-ladder-position}

\rmark{R14} Churn by precision:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
model & Q8\_0 & Q6\_K & Q5\_K\_M & Q4\_K\_M & Q3\_K\_M & Q2\_K \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
llamaguard3-8b & 1 & 8 & 14 & 18 & 29 & 84 \\
qwen3guard-06b & 4 & 2 & 13 & 11 & 38 & \textbf{485} \\
qwen3guard-4b & 0 & 2 & 2 & 4 & 7 & 30 \\
shieldgemma-2b & 3 & 6 & 11 & 18 & 41 & 48 \\
shieldgemma-9b & 6 & 8 & 7 & 17 & 26 & 84 \\

Churn rises with compression, as expected, and \textbf{Qwen3Guard 0.6B at \texttt{Q2\_K} churns 485 of 1,000} --- a

is not the finding.}

\subsection{5.8 The mechanism reaches guards --- measured, not assumed}\label{58-the-mechanism-reaches-guards--measured-not-assumed}

\warn{} \textbf{An earlier draft of this paper said we could not test this. We since did.}
{[}MarginShrink{]}\textquotesingle s law is fitted on \textbf{16 generative instruct models} where every decision is a
next-token choice between two continuations. \textbf{No guard classifier appears in their study, nor in
{[}Certify{]} or {[}QualityProxy{]}.} A guard\textquotesingle s verdict \emph{is} the decision rather than a token inside a
generation, so whether the law reaches that object was untested by anyone.

\textbf{Pre-registered at \texttt{34dc31e7} before any logit was captured.} Two guards $\times$ seven precisions
$\times$ 1,000 items, RTN quantization at group size 64, served through transformers. Zero null margins.

\warn{} \textbf{These cells are not comparable to the ladder in \S{}5.1--\S{}5.7, and the
pre-registration said so in advance.} Different serving stack --- transformers against
Ollama/GGUF --- and a different quantizer --- RTN against K-quants. \textbf{Only the law is
comparable.} The GGUF stack cannot expose logits, so a margin cannot be measured on it at all; that
is why this could not simply be run on the cells above. \textbf{What follows establishes that the law
governs guard classifiers as a class. It does not establish that these coefficients describe the
GGUF cells.}

\rmark{R15} \textbf{H1 --- the functional form transfers.} Multiplicative beats constant-additive by BIC in
\textbf{5 of 6 cells in both guards}. The single additive win in each model falls at a precision where
there is essentially no damage --- 5 bits for the 0.6B, 8 bits for the 4B --- where the two
accounts are near-indistinguishable.

\rmark{R16} \textbf{H2 --- the collapse is real; the registered check was the wrong instrument for it.} The
surviving fraction \emph{c}:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
bits & Qwen3Guard-0.6B & Qwen3Guard-4B \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
8 & 0.996 & 0.999 \\
6 & 1.012 & 1.013 \\
5 & 0.999 & 0.986 \\
4 & \textbf{0.876} & 0.955 \\
3 & \textbf{0.014} & \textbf{0.680} \\
2 & \textbf{0.006} & \textbf{0.003} \\
\end{longtable}

\warn{} \textbf{The pre-registered check was strict monotonicity in \emph{c}, and it fails in both
models} --- \emph{c} rises from 0.996 to 1.012 between 8 and 6 bits, with standard errors of 0.0007
and 0.0014, so the rise is real rather than noise. \textbf{Reported as registered, and as failed.}

\textbf{The substantive claim nonetheless holds, and the registered test does not capture it.} The wiggle
sits at precisions where \emph{c} $\approx$ 1 and nothing is damaged; the collapse it was meant to detect is
unmistakable below 4 bits. \textbf{This is a point-estimate ordering check firing on a real but immaterial
movement}, and the standing correction applies: register the test, not the direction.

\textbf{The collapse point is model-dependent, and the smaller guard fails a full bit earlier.} The 0.6B
is already destroyed at 3 bits (\emph{c} = 0.014) where the 4B retains two-thirds of its margin
(\emph{c} = 0.680). Both reach \emph{c} $\approx$ 0 at 2 bits, matching {[}MarginShrink{]}\textquotesingle s reported median of 0.00.

\rmark{R17} \textbf{H3 --- the flip predictor transfers, at lower error than in their setting.} With
(\emph{c}, \emph{b}, $\sigma$) fitted on \textbf{margins only and never on flips}, their predictor gives a mean
absolute error of \textbf{0.75 percentage points} for the 0.6B and \textbf{0.94} for the 4B, against their
\textbf{1.7pp median} across 1,270 cells, and inside the pre-registered 5pp bound.

\textbf{This is expected rather than impressive.} A guard\textquotesingle s decision is a single binary verdict on a fixed
input, so there is less for the residual to absorb than in a next-token choice inside a generation
--- and \textbf{fewer cells also means less opportunity to be wrong.}

\rmark{R18} \textbf{H4 --- direction is model-specific and reverses within a ladder.} The fitted push \emph{b}:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
bits & Qwen3Guard-0.6B & Qwen3Guard-4B \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
8 & +0.090 & +0.050 \\
6 & +0.080 & +0.214 \\
5 & +0.754 & +0.448 \\
4 & \textbf{$-$0.348} & +0.136 \\
3 & \textbf{$-$0.148} & +0.058 \\
2 & \textbf{+1.988} & \textbf{$-$1.120} \\
\end{longtable}

Positive \emph{b} pushes toward \textbf{Unsafe} --- safety-conservative, over-blocking. Negative pushes
toward \textbf{Safe} --- safety-adverse, admitting harm. \textbf{The two guards disagree in sign at 4 and 3
bits}, and \textbf{both reverse sign within their own ladder}: the 0.6B at 4 bits and again at 2, the 4B
only at 2.

\textbf{\S{}5.2 observed exactly this behaviorally and could not explain it.} ShieldGemma 2B is purely
usability-adverse at \texttt{Q4\_K\_M} and \texttt{Q3\_K\_M}, then 47-to-1 safety-adverse at \texttt{Q2\_K}. \textbf{The fitted \emph{b}
is the shape of the explanation --- a directional push whose sign is not fixed across
precisions.}

\warn{} \textbf{The shape, not the instance.} ShieldGemma is not among the two guards instrumented
here, and the stack differs. \textbf{This makes the mechanism available to \S{}5.2; it does not fit it.}

\textbf{None of the law is ours} (\S{}1). What is ours is the measurement that it reaches this object,
and the negative result in \texttt{R16}.

\section{6. What a deployer should take from this}\label{6-what-a-deployer-should-take-from-this}

\textbf{Ask which direction, not how much.} A single churn figure for ShieldGemma 9B is 148 items and tells
you nothing you can act on; the decomposition --- 144 unsafe$\rightarrow$\allowbreak{}safe against 4 --- tells you the model has
become less safe rather than noisier. \textbf{Any guard quantization report that does not separate the two
directions is withholding the operative number.}

\textbf{Do not infer direction from precision.} ShieldGemma 2B is over-blocking at \texttt{Q4\_K\_M} and
under-blocking at \texttt{Q2\_K}. \textbf{The ladder position does not tell you which failure you are buying.}

\textbf{Size the evaluation from churn, and measure churn first.} Guard accuracy does not predict the
requirement: our worst and mid-range guards need identical evidence (\S{}5.4).

\textbf{Declare a margin.} {[}Certify{]}\textquotesingle s audit found none of 16 eligible published equivalence claims did.
Their five-line standard applies here unchanged: declare a margin, run the paired test, report churn
beside net delta, cite the sample size you met, release per-item outputs.

\textbf{Flip risk is predictable from margins, without running the ladder.} {[}MarginShrink{]}\textquotesingle s
predictor, fitted on margins alone, hit guard flip rates to under one percentage point
(\S{}5.8). \textbf{If your serving stack exposes logits, you can estimate what a precision will cost
you before you deploy it} --- and if it does not, that is itself a reason to prefer one that
does.

\textbf{And measure your own floor.} Ours differed by more than an order of magnitude depending on which
prior corpus we imported it from, and only measurement settled it (\S{}5.5).

\section{7. Limitations}\label{7-limitations}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{The instrument is not ours} (\S{}0, \S{}1), and neither is the cross-scheme audit.
  1b. \warn{} \textbf{We do not extrapolate from their atlas, and may not.} {[}Certify{]} \S{}4.4 and \S{}9 are explicit
  that it is \emph{"the public record of compression evaluation, not a census of quantization"} ---
  community quantizations of 2023-era models conditioned on leaderboard coverage, plus one vendor\textquotesingle s
  releases evaluated by that vendor. \textbf{Our comparisons against their S1/S2 shares in \S{}5.5 are
  against that record, not against quantization in general}, and our own requirement figures come
  from discordance we measured, not from their rows.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{F16} is the reference, not the truth.} Every delta is movement away from a model\textquotesingle s own
  half-precision behavior, which is not itself validated as correct.
\item
  \textbf{One conversion pipeline, one serving stack.} All ladders come from a single publisher\textquotesingle s GGUF
  conversions served through one stack, deliberately, to hold the pipeline constant. \textbf{Nothing here
  generalizes to AWQ, GPTQ or NF4}, and \S{}0 explains why we did not extend.
\item
  \textbf{The floor is measured for one model at one precision} (\S{}5.5). Floors are model-dependent, so
  the other four models\textquotesingle{} comparisons rest on an assumption.
\item
  \textbf{The corpus is adversarially weighted} (\S{}3), so absolute rates are not deployment rates.
\item
  \textbf{H1\textquotesingle s direction was known before the study was designed} (\S{}1).
\item
  \textbf{A mechanism exists and it is not ours; we do not test whether it reaches guards.} \warn{} \textbf{An
  earlier draft of this paper claimed the direction was unexplained. That was wrong.}
  \textbf{{[}MarginShrink{]} supply the mechanism}: compression damage is \textbf{proportional, not additive} ---
  the quantized margin follows \emph{m$'$} = \emph{c\textperiodcentered{}m} + \emph{b} + $\varepsilon$, with the surviving fraction \emph{c} collapsing
  from a median 0.86 at 4 bits to 0.33 at 3 and \textbf{0.00 at 2}. Confident decisions therefore lose the
  \emph{same fraction} of their margin as marginal ones and cross zero too, which refutes the fixed-noise
  intuition; they exclude that whole class with a parameter-free bound that \textbf{107 of 183 measured
  steps violate}. The directional push \emph{b} is the direction term. From this they derive a flip
  predictor, \texttt{P(flip\textbar{}m)\ =\ $\Phi$($-$(cm+b)\textperiodcentered{}sign(m)/$\sigma$)}, fitted on margins rather than flips, with a
  \textbf{median held-out error of 1.7 percentage points} across 1,270 cells.
  \textbf{We tested whether that law governs guard classifiers, and it does} (\S{}5.8). Their 16
  models are all generative instruct models and every decision is a next-token choice between two
  continuations; \textbf{no guard classifier appears in their study}, and a guard\textquotesingle s verdict is the
  decision rather than a token inside a generation. The functional form, the collapse and the flip
  predictor all transfer, the last at under 1pp mean error.
  \warn{} \textbf{But on a different serving stack, and this bounds what \S{}5.8 may be used
  for.} Margins require logits, which the GGUF stack does not expose, so the test ran on
  transformers with RTN quantization. \textbf{The law is established for guard classifiers as a class;
  that it describes the specific cells in \S{}5.1--\S{}5.7 remains an inference.}
  \warn{} \textbf{And its pre-registered monotonicity check failed}, reported as failed in \texttt{R16}.
  \textbf{Two guards, one family, one corpus, one quantizer.} ShieldGemma and Llama Guard are not
  instrumented, and they are the two families \S{}5.2 finds most directionally extreme. \textbf{We fit
  the push \emph{b}; we do not explain why it points where it does, or why it reverses.}
  For completeness, the probes that \emph{did} fail are {[}QualityProxy{]} \S{}4.4\textquotesingle s four: entropy shift
  (\emph{p} = 0.606), calibration drift (all \textbar{}\emph{r}\textbar{} \textless{} 0.09), refusal-direction geometry (cosine above 0.97
  in every quantized cell), and safety-neuron error --- real at 1.39$\times$, \emph{p} = 4.89 $\times$ 10$^{-}$$^{7}$, but
  \textbf{global rather than regime-specific}.
\item
  \textbf{Five models, three families.} ShieldGemma contributes two of the five, and its two members
  supply both the most safety-adverse row and the mid-ladder reversal, so \S{}5.2\textquotesingle s spread rests
  partly on one family.
\item
  \textbf{Single seed per cell} for the 35 ladder cells; only the floor condition was replicated.
\end{enumerate}

\section{8. Artifact}\label{8-artifact}

Per-item verdicts for all 35 cells and all 8 floor replicates; the corpus with its hash; the
pre-registration and its addendum with both hashes; the analyzer, the pooled-ratio and dual-floor
follow-up, and the floor analyzer. \textbf{Every statistic in \S{}5.1 through \S{}5.4 and \S{}5.6 is reproducible
from the released verdicts with no GPU.}

\textbf{\S{}5.8 adds} the per-item decision margins for both guards at all seven precisions, its
pre-registration and hash, the margin-capture job and the analyzer --- which, as the
pre-registration required, \textbf{was written before any logit was captured}.

\textbf{Total new compute: 30.4 GPU-minutes on A10G for the floor replicates (\$0.56), plus the
\S{}5.8 margin capture on A100-40GB (approximately \$0.70).} The 35-cell
analysis cost nothing --- it is a re-analysis of verdicts collected by earlier experiments in this
program. \textbf{The pipeline had estimated \textasciitilde20 GPU-hours; the literature check removed the part that would
have consumed them, and {[}Certify{]}\textquotesingle s calibration-draw result showed that part would have been an
artifact.}
